standard.title: Characters and settings across contexts
standard.description: discuss how characters and settings are connected in literature created by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors and illustrators
standard.prior_knowledge: Students discuss how language and images create characters, settings and events in literature from First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors (AC9E1LE01). They have not yet examined how the connection between character and setting varies across different cultural and national literary traditions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can discuss how characters and settings are connected in literature from First Nations Australian, wide-ranging Australian and world authors and illustrators.

nodes.label: Character-setting connections
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how a character belongs to or is shaped by the setting they inhabit in a literary text.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one way a character in a familiar text is connected to their setting — e.g. the character's actions, knowledge or challenges are shaped by where they are.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss character-setting connections across several texts — narrative, picture book, short story — identifying how setting shapes what characters do, what they know and what problems they face.
wider: Compare two texts with very different settings and discuss how each shapes the types of characters who inhabit them
Discuss how the Australian landscape shapes Australian characters differently from European fairy-tale settings
success_criteria: Student can identify a specific connection between a character and their setting in a given text.
Student can explain how the setting influences at least one aspect of the character's behaviour or experience.

nodes.label: World literature traditions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss how character-setting connections are used in literature from different world traditions and identify recurring patterns.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a recurring character-setting pattern in a familiar world literary tradition — e.g. children in forests in European fairy tales, royalty in castles.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss recurring character-setting patterns across several world literary traditions, exploring why certain settings recur with certain types of characters and what cultural meanings they carry.
wider: Compare the settings used for similar character archetypes (e.g. powerful figures, lost children) across European, Asian and African literary traditions
Investigate how illustrators from different cultural backgrounds depict settings differently for similar story types

response_modes.reason: Understanding that character-setting conventions vary across world traditions requires students to accumulate examples from different literary traditions. Schema for 'what is typical for this tradition' only forms once enough varied examples have been experienced. Breadth of literary traditions is the productive investment.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: World literature traditions offer genuinely rich content — each new tradition (European fairy tale, Japanese folk tale, African oral story) adds a distinct set of character-setting conventions. Advancing students can begin to see these conventions as cultural constructs rather than universal truths.
success_criteria: Student can identify a recurring character-setting pattern in at least one literary tradition.
Student can explain why certain characters and settings recur together in that tradition.

nodes.label: First Nations Australian literature
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss how First Nations Australian authors use character-setting connections that reflect relationships with Country and Place.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a character-setting connection in a text by a First Nations Australian author and discuss one way it differs from or is similar to connections in other texts they have read.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how First Nations Australian authors depict characters whose identities and actions are connected to Country, Place and community; recognise recurring character types in texts by First Nations Australian authors.
wider: Compare how the same geographical setting (e.g. a specific country or region) is depicted by a First Nations Australian author vs a non-First Nations author, discussing differences in the relationship between character and place
Explore how illustrations in texts by First Nations Australian illustrators visually represent character-Country connections
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Australian literary traditions offer distinct and enriching content for understanding character-setting relationships — particularly the concept of Country as connected to identity. This is meaningful widening that connects to broader cultural understanding.
success_criteria: Student can identify a character-setting connection in a text by a First Nations Australian author.
Student can discuss at least one feature of how this connection differs from or enriches their understanding beyond other literary traditions.
